stem: In Python, 7 / 2 gives 3.5 and 7 // 2 gives 3. In C and Java, what does 7 / 2 give when both operands are int?

options.text: 3.5, the same as Python's /
3, because / on two ints is integer division
A compile error; you must write 7 // 2
4, because the result is rounded to nearest

explanation: C and Java choose the operation from the OPERAND types, not the result you want. Two ints means integer division, truncating toward zero — so 7 / 2 is 3. Python 3 went the other way and made / always true division. There is no // operator in C or Java. To get 3.5 you must make an operand floating point: 7 / 2.0, or (double) a / b. Pattern: coming from Python, assume every / between two ints silently truncates.

distractorRationale.a: That is Python 3's behaviour specifically; C and Java predate it and kept the C convention.
distractorRationale.c: // is a comment in C and Java, so 7 // 2 would comment out the rest of the line.
distractorRationale.d: Neither language rounds; the fractional part is discarded, not rounded.

stem: In Python, -7 % 3 evaluates to 2. What does -7 % 3 evaluate to in C and Java?

options.text: 2, the same as Python
-1, because the result takes the sign of the dividend
1, because the sign is discarded
It is undefined behaviour

explanation: Python's % returns a result with the sign of the DIVISOR, so -7 % 3 is 2. C and Java return a result with the sign of the DIVIDEND, so -7 % 3 is -1. This is the nastiest difference in this set because nothing crashes: any code that assumes a non-negative remainder — hashing into a bucket, wrapping a circular index — silently produces a negative index. The fix is ((a % n) + n) % n.

distractorRationale.a: This is exactly the wrong assumption to carry over, and it fails silently rather than loudly.
distractorRationale.c: Neither language takes an absolute value; the sign is meaningful.
distractorRationale.d: It is fully specified in both languages (C99 onwards); only the convention differs from Python.

stem: You want the last element of an array of length n. In Python you would write arr[-1]. What happens in C if you write arr[-1]?

options.text: It returns the last element, as in Python
It reads the memory just before the array — undefined behaviour, often garbage
It raises an IndexError at runtime
It returns 0, the default value

explanation: C computes arr[i] as *(arr + i) with no bounds check at all, so arr[-1] reads the word before the array. That is undefined behaviour: it may print garbage, may appear to work, and may crash — and it will often behave differently under a debugger than in the test harness. Write arr[n - 1]. Java at least throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, so the failure is loud there; in C it is silent.

distractorRationale.a: Negative indexing is a Python convenience; C has no concept of it.
distractorRationale.c: That is Java's behaviour (an exception) and Python's; C performs no check whatsoever.
distractorRationale.d: C never zero-fills on an out-of-bounds read; it reads whatever is there.

stem: You need to build a string character by character inside a loop in Java. Which approach is correct and efficient?

options.text: result += c inside the loop, as you would in Python
result.charAt(i) = c, assigning into the string
Use a StringBuilder and call append(c), then toString() at the end
Declare the String with a fixed length and index into it

explanation: Java Strings are immutable, so += builds a brand new String on every iteration — quadratic time, and a classic timeout on a large input. StringBuilder mutates one buffer and converts once at the end. Python's str is also immutable, but CPython optimises += in some cases and problem sizes rarely expose it, so the habit survives until it meets Java.

distractorRationale.a: It compiles and is correct, but it is O(n squared) and will time out on a large input.
distractorRationale.b: charAt returns a value; it is not assignable. Strings cannot be modified in place at all.
distractorRationale.d: A String has no pre-allocated, writable buffer — that is what StringBuilder provides.

stem: In Python, if arr: tests whether a list is non-empty. In Java, what does if (arr) do for an int[] named arr?

options.text: It tests whether the array has any elements
It tests whether the reference is non-null
It fails to compile, because the condition must be a boolean
It tests whether the first element is non-zero

explanation: Java requires the condition of an if to be a boolean; there is no truthiness. if (arr) is a compile error, and so is if (n) for an int. You must write an explicit comparison: arr.length > 0, or arr != null. C is the opposite trap — it accepts any scalar, so if (arr) compiles and is almost always true (a non-null pointer), which silently does the wrong thing.

distractorRationale.a: That is Python's semantics; Java has no implicit emptiness test.
distractorRationale.b: A null check is what you often MEAN, but you must write it explicitly as arr != null.
distractorRationale.d: No language in this family does that; it is not a plausible semantics, only a plausible guess.

stem: Python lets you swap with a, b = b, a. What is the correct equivalent in C or Java?

options.text: a = b; b = a;
int tmp = a; a = b; b = tmp;
swap(a, b);
a, b = b, a;

explanation: Neither language has tuple assignment, so a swap needs a temporary. "a = b; b = a;" is the bug this question exists for: it compiles, runs, and leaves both variables holding b — the original value of a is destroyed by the first statement. Pattern: any two-statement swap without a temporary has already lost one of the values.

distractorRationale.a: This is the classic broken swap. It compiles and silently loses a's original value.
distractorRationale.c: C++ has std::swap, but plain C does not, and Java has no such function for primitives.
distractorRationale.d: The comma here is the comma operator in C, not tuple assignment; it does not swap.

stem: You want the 0-25 alphabet position of a lowercase character c. In Python you would write ord(c) - ord('a'). What is the C equivalent?

options.text: ord(c) - ord('a')
c - 'a', because a char is already an integer type
(int) c - (int) "a"
atoi(c) - atoi('a')

explanation: In C and Java, char IS an integer type, so arithmetic works directly: c - 'a' gives the offset with no conversion function. Python needs ord() because its str has no numeric value. Note the quotes carefully: 'a' is a character literal, "a" is a string (a pointer in C) — mixing them is a common error for someone used to Python, where both quote styles mean the same thing.

distractorRationale.a: ord() is a Python builtin; it does not exist in C.
distractorRationale.c: "a" is a string literal, so this subtracts a pointer value, not a character code.
distractorRationale.d: atoi parses a numeric string like "42"; it is unrelated to character codes.

stem: Python lets you write result = [] then result.append(x) as many times as you like. What is the closest correct approach in C?

options.text: Declare int result[]; and append with result[i++] = x
Declare an array large enough for the worst case and track the count yourself
Use result.append(x) after including <stdlib.h>
Arrays in C grow automatically when you write past the end

explanation: C arrays have a fixed size fixed at declaration, and there is no length field and no append. The standard competitive-programming approach is to declare the worst case (int result[1000];) and keep your own int count. The alternatives are malloc/realloc, or C++'s std::vector. Pattern: in C, every array needs a companion variable holding how many elements are actually in use, because the array itself does not know.

distractorRationale.a: int result[]; without a size is not a valid declaration for a local array, and i++ does not allocate space.
distractorRationale.c: C has no methods on arrays; stdlib.h provides malloc, not append.
distractorRationale.d: Writing past the end is undefined behaviour — it corrupts adjacent memory rather than growing anything.

stem: Python's s[1:4] gives characters at indices 1, 2 and 3. What is the Java equivalent?

options.text: s.substring(1, 4), which is also end-exclusive
s.substring(1, 3), because Java's end index is inclusive
s.slice(1, 4)
s[1:4], which Java also supports

explanation: Java's substring(begin, end) uses the same half-open convention as Python: begin is included, end is excluded, so substring(1, 4) returns indices 1, 2 and 3. The trap is assuming it is inclusive and passing 3, which silently returns one character too few. C has no slicing at all — you copy a range manually and terminate it yourself.

distractorRationale.b: This is the off-by-one the question exists for; Java's end index is exclusive, like Python's.
distractorRationale.c: slice is a JavaScript method; Java uses substring.
distractorRationale.d: Java has no slice syntax; brackets on a String are a compile error.

stem: A C function declares int count; inside a loop body and then does count++ without assigning it first. What happens?

options.text: count starts at 0, as an unassigned integer would in Python
count holds whatever was in that memory — undefined behaviour, and it may appear to work
The compiler refuses to build it
count is automatically None until assigned

explanation: A local variable in C is not initialised; it contains whatever bytes were already on the stack. It often happens to be 0 in a simple test and non-zero once the surrounding code changes, which is why this bug passes locally and fails in the grader. Always initialise: int count = 0;. Java is stricter — it refuses to compile a read of an uninitialised local — and Python has no declaration step at all, so the habit never forms.

distractorRationale.a: Python has no uninitialised state; a name either exists or raises NameError. C makes no such guarantee.
distractorRationale.c: Most compilers only warn (with -Wall), and the default build often says nothing at all.
distractorRationale.d: There is no None in C, and no null for a primitive int.
